_README: approach_variants for multi-route areas in the Mountain Loop Highway corridor, the central Cascades and the Olympics.
Scope: every route in the 13 target areas that had NO approach_variants on the live table at the time of writing.

Live counts differ from the worklist that was handed over — re-queried and used the live numbers: M&M Wall holds 5 routes (not 4), Goose Egg 7 (not 2), Morning Star 4 (not 3), Pinto Rock's West Face 3 (not 2), and Three Fingers' South Peak row ALREADY carries approach_variants, so 39 rows were in scope rather than the 30 the worklist implied.
31 routes written, 8 skipped, 1 out of scope. Every entry carries an 'area' equal to the live routes.area_id, verified mechanically against a fresh read.
READ-ONLY. Nothing was written to the database and nothing in the repo was touched.

WHY THESE AREAS: every one holds several routes off one trailhead, so 'you are at the right trailhead' does not mean 'you are under the right line'. Each baseFinding therefore names something you can see, touch or count at the foot of the climb, and where the row supports it, a negative marker naming the neighbouring line you have reached by mistake.

ROUTE IDS LIE — as expected, most of these ids are derived from the route NAME and say nothing about the peak. Every one was resolved through its area_id and the resolution is stated in each entry's _why. The worst offenders here: wa_west_face, wa_south_ridge and wa_accidental_discharge_east_face all sit on Gunsight South Peak; wa_northwest_face_4 sits on Little Big Chief; wa_nest_route, wa_spectacle_route and wa_wild_wild_west all sit on Pinto Rock's West Face; wa_three_fingers_r1 and _r2 are the North and Middle summits of Three Fingers.

NO hours, distances or elevation gains were written into any variant. Several of these areas store one-way and round-trip figures side by side on rows that share a trailhead (see _DEFECTS), so any figure written here would have been an average nobody published.
NO source names, URLs, author names or years appear in any name/season/notes/baseFinding/hazards field. Provenance is in _sources only.

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
approach_variants.season: Late June to September, once the gully has melted out and the lower pitches have dried; the highway over the pass is gated shut all winter, so there is no cold-season access at all.
approach_variants.notes: Park at the roadside pullout near milepost 166 and start straight uphill to the north — there is no trail and no sign. Head for the talus at the foot of the gully that splits the wall; the gully forces you briefly out to the left before you rejoin it higher. Two ledge systems break the wall. The lower one comes first; keep going past it to the upper ledge, where the long routes start. The wall faces due south and there is no shade below the cave, so on a hot day the approach is the hottest part of the route.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Get onto the UPPER of the wall's two ledge systems — not the first ledge you meet coming up the gully. Then walk right. This is the right-hand line on the wall and the huge cave that gives the wall its name is directly above you, not off to one side. The check on the ground is the first pitch itself: a left-facing corner about forty metres long that runs to a stance directly beneath a pair of TWIN CRACKS SLANTING LEFT. Count the corner's length and look for the twin cracks above the first stance — that pair is unique on this section of wall. Negative markers: if the corner above you is short, slabby and only about twenty-five metres to its anchor, you have drifted left into the middle of the wall and are under the eleven-pitch line; if you are standing on a treed ledge that two separate lines leave from, you are further left again. And if the cave is high above you but you are on a narrow ledge with one lone bolt at ground level, you never left the lower ledge and are on the three-pitch apron route.
hazards: Loose talus and creek-bed footing in the approach gully, with rockfall from anyone above you in it
Full south-facing sun on the whole approach with no shade until the cave
Water and seepage on the lower pitches persists into early summer in wet years
The highway is gated closed through winter and well into spring, so the approach can be unreachable by car

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
approach_variants.season: July to September; the highway over the pass is gated shut through winter and into spring, so the wall is car-inaccessible for roughly half the year.
approach_variants.notes: From the roadside pullout near milepost 166, go directly uphill to the north through talus and forest toward the gully below the wall, taking the forced dogleg out left and back in. Pass the lower ledge and keep going to the upper ledge. There is an exposed easy-fifth step in the gully on the way, so this is not a walk with your hands in your pockets. Rockfall in the gully is worse when another party is above you and worse again after rain.
approach_variants.baseFinding: On the upper ledge, work to the CENTRE of the wall — this line is neither the right-hand cave line nor the apron below. The start is a treed ledge, and it is shared: two routes leave from the same spot, so identify it by the ledge and the trees, then identify the ROUTE by where you stop. The first pitch here is short — a slabby left-facing corner, about twenty-five metres, ending at a belay well below the first roof. Negative markers: if you run the same corner out to more than sixty metres and finish at a pin-and-gear anchor tucked under a roof, you are on the free variation of the old aid line, which shares this ground; if the corner you started up is forty metres long and leads to a stance under twin left-slanting cracks, you are on the right-hand cave line; and if you are on a narrow ledge below the whole wall with a single bolt beside you, you stopped one ledge too low.
hazards: Loose talus and an exposed easy-fifth step in the approach gully
Rockfall in the gully, particularly with parties above or after rain
South-facing aspect gives full-day sun and real heat in summer
Two routes leave the same treed ledge — confirm which anchor you are heading for before you commit to a rope length

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the shared treed-ledge start
approach_variants.season: June to September, once the gully is clear; no access while the highway over the pass is gated for winter.
approach_variants.notes: Same walk-in as the wall's other long routes: from the pullout near milepost 166 go straight uphill north into the talus below the gully, out left where it forces you, back into the gully, past the lower ledge, and on to the upper ledge. Allow more time than the distance suggests — the ground is talus, loose, and steepens near the top.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The start is the treed ledge in the middle of the wall, and it is NOT unique to this route — the eleven-pitch centre line begins from the same place. What identifies this climb is the first rope length. Stay in the left-facing corner and run it well past the point where a short pitch would end: this line's first belay is a PIN-AND-GEAR ANCHOR set beneath a roof, more than twice the length of the neighbouring route's first pitch, and there is no bolted station at the short-pitch height on this line. Above, the giveaway is the fixed gear: old pitons left from the original aid ascent stud the line and appear on no other route on the wall — treat every one of them as decoration, not protection. Negative markers: if you clip into a bolted anchor about twenty-five metres up, you have taken the centre line's first belay; if you started from a broad ledge on the wall's right-hand side beneath the big cave with twin left-slanting cracks above, you are on the cave route entirely.
hazards: Loose talus in the approach gully and rockfall from parties above
Old fixed pitons from the original aid ascent remain in place and must not be trusted
Very few repeat ascents, so expect route-finding uncertainty from the first pitch onward
The cave traverse higher up holds loose rock and stays cold and damp

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the LOWER ledge
approach_variants.season: June to September; the highway over the pass is gated closed for the winter and the approach is unreachable by car until it reopens.
approach_variants.notes: From the roadside pullout near milepost 166, head straight uphill to the north into the talus below the gully, take the short forced dogleg out left, and rejoin the gully. This route is the one climb here that does NOT need the full walk-in — stop at the first ledge system rather than continuing to the upper one. Everything above you is a different, much longer route, so it is worth being certain you are low before you rack up.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Stop at the LOWER of the wall's two ledge systems — the first one you reach, before the talus steepens for the last stretch. This line climbs the apron BELOW the wall's long routes, not the wall proper. Walk the lower ledge and look for a SINGLE BELAY BOLT on a small ledge: it is the only piece of fixed gear at ground level here, and it marks the start. Confirm it from the rock immediately above: the first pitch is easy, taking small wires in cracks as well as bolts, so if the wall above your head is steep, clean and blank you are in the wrong place. Sight upward for the second confirmation — the start of the right-hand cave route is directly above you, and the tennis-court-sized cave that names the wall is higher still, not overhead. Negative marker: if you are standing on a broad ledge with several routes' worth of bolted anchors along it and the cave dominates the view above, you have carried on to the UPPER ledge and are roughly ten minutes above this climb; drop back down the gully.
hazards: Loose talus in the approach gully
Rockfall from parties on the long routes above the lower ledge
South-facing exposure — the apron bakes in full summer sun with no shade
The single ground-level bolt is the only marker; there is no cairn or path along the lower ledge

approach_variants.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
approach_variants.notes: There is no way to walk to this climb. Do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are looking for a TWO-BOLT ANCHOR sitting on the midway ledge, and the trees are what place it: the anchor is on the ledge BELOW a stand of trees, not level with them and not above them. Traverse LEFT along the ledge until the trees are above you and the two bolts are at your feet. Confirm it from the rock: the first pitch off this anchor is a technical corner with loose chockstones at its hardest moves, so if what rises from your anchor is a clean face or a slab you are at the wrong station. Negative markers: if the anchor you have clipped is one of the bolted rappel stations belonging to the route you just climbed, you have not traversed at all; if the trees are still off to your left, you have not traversed far enough.
hazards: No ground approach — a retreat means reversing or rappelling somebody else's route
Loose and deteriorating rock on the lowest pitches and again high on the line
Belays are bolted but not all of them are rigged for rappel, so this is not a line to bail down
Everything below you is occupied ground; manage rockfall onto parties on the route you climbed in on

approach_variants.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
approach_variants.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it, and note that this is also the line most parties use to get back DOWN afterwards.
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the midway ledge, traverse LEFT — further than from the centre line — until you find the TWO-BOLT ANCHOR set on the ledge directly BELOW a stand of trees. The trees are the test: below them, not beside them. The first pitch above the anchor is a technical corner holding loose chockstones at the crux, which distinguishes it from the clean faces either side. Negative markers: if you are still passing bolted rappel stations that belong to the route you climbed up, keep traversing; if you have reached ground where the ledge system ends and the wall closes down, you have gone past it.
hazards: No ground approach; escape means rappelling a neighbouring line
Loose and deteriorating rock low and high on the route
Not all belays are rappel-rigged, so plan the descent before you leave the ledge
Long leftward traverse on a ledge with loose material on it
